source.title: An Interpretable and Scalable Framework for Evaluating Large Language Models
source.authors: Xin-Hao Qu; Qiang Heng; Hao Zeng; Xiaoqian Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study compares benchmark-derived model ability across model sizes, providing a different-measure test of whether evaluated capabilities tend to improve with scale. It does not test held-out pretraining loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The study reports that cBMM-recovered ability on MATH-500 trends upward across release time and that larger models generally have stronger reasoning performance; these results bear on V6. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy, fit scaling exponents, test extrapolation, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its stated consistency with published scaling laws is contextual, not a test of those laws. Figure 4's ability-versus-average-accuracy relationship and Figure 5's ranking comparisons concern ranking agreement rather than performance growth with scale, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper: an MM-based IRT estimator (cBMM) for benchmark evaluation. The scaling remarks in Section 4.2 are a sanity check of the recovered abilities, which the authors call consistent with Kaplan and Chinchilla. They are not a test of the scaling claim. The comparison is qualitative and figure-only, across an uncontrolled mix of ~70 models of different families, data, post-training and distillation, grouped into three coarse size tiers. No loss, no fitted curve and no prediction from scale or loss is reported. The expected scaling pattern is used to validate the method, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors' main conclusion is that cBMM gives orders-of-magnitude speedups (41x–86x on the leaderboard suites, up to 200x in simulation) with comparable or better estimation accuracy. They state its ability estimates are consistent with parametric scaling laws and that item parameters match human difficulty annotations. The scaling consistency is presented as validation of the method, not as a scaling result.
record.recipe_differences: This is an IRT-based benchmark-ability evaluation, not a held-out cross-entropy scaling-law sweep. It compares recovered ability across existing models rather than fitting loss curves or testing compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ability trend is considered across model size tiers and release dates; 01-ai/Yi-34B is identified as a deviation associated with training-token-to-parameter balance.

fits_no_version.finding: cBMM-recovered MATH-500 ability rises with release date within each size tier (0–7B, 7–20B, >20B). Larger tiers show higher overall placements and peaks; this is qualitative and figure-only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benchmark ability of open LLMs at fixed size tier improves over release time.

fits_no_version.finding: Across seven suites, Spearman agreement between cBMM ability and average accuracy falls as the coefficient of variation of item discrimination rises. This holds for the top 20% of models and for all models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Agreement between IRT-derived ability rankings and average-accuracy rankings varies with benchmark-item discrimination heterogeneity.

fits_no_version.finding: Ranking flows on MATH, MMLU-Pro and GPQA show larger discrepancies as discrimination heterogeneity grows. Qwen2-Math-72B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B shift upward under cBMM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benchmark item heterogeneity can change model rankings relative to average accuracy.

record.problems: For the scaling-related result, the text gives qualitative trends rather than numerical model-ability values or fitted relationships; Figure 2 is the only locator for those values. The benchmark-ability results are from MATH-500 and do not measure pretraining loss or establish predictive performance across downstream tasks generally.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant result rows were left out.

untested.parts: No compute-allocation sweep; the Yi remark is an unmeasured attribution.
Only a qualitative size-tier sanity check on MATH-500 across heterogeneous models. There is no controlled scale sweep, no predictive fit, and no loss–performance relation.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V6 'supports' labels are removed. The scaling observation is a qualitative validation check on an uncontrolled model collection. Rows r1–r3 describe trends over release time, not over scale. The Yi-34B explanation is the authors' attribution, not a measurement.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute curves are measured.
No power-law fits on small runs or loss predictions for larger runs are reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token counts are measured.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No cross-modal or alternative-training-regime loss scaling is tested.

Tests benchmark-derived ability across model sizes on MATH-500, but does not test performance prediction from pretraining loss, provide fitted predictive curves, or establish the relationship across downstream tasks generally.
No alternative fitting methods or setup choices for scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations are compared.

rows.operation_detail: Compared cBMM-recovered ability with the general size-related trend
rows.measure: cBMM-recovered model ability θ̂ relative to the general parametric scaling trend
rows.note: The text identifies a deviation and attributes it primarily to the Yi series' disproportionate scaling of training tokens relative to parameters; it does not state the numerical direction or magnitude.
rows.check: The text names a 'notable deviation' for Yi-34B but gives no direction or magnitude. The attribution to its token/parameter ratio is the authors' post-hoc explanation citing [60], not a measured result. 'partial' is unsupported.
